display_title: Important task, noval model but not strong enough baselines

content.title: Important task, noval model but not strong enough baselines
content.review:
This paper investigates augmenting neural text classification models with learned cluster centers. The trainable cluster centroid parameters are initialized from K-means/GMM results on pre-trained word embeddings. The cluster centers also align with latent representations induced from a Variational Autoencoders (VAE) model via an unsupervised clustering objective. Then this paper proposes a clustering-token interaction layer that assigns each token in a sentence to cluster centroids and integrates cluster-aware information into token representations. The text classification model and VAE model are trained jointly. 

Pros:
- This paper has a thorough experimental plan, comparing it with different CNN/LSTM/transformer/GCN baselines on several benchmarks. It shows that the proposed model has improvements over baselines, and also does a detailed visualization analysis.

Cons:
- It could be better to compare with more powerful pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) on the text classification tasks.
- CluE-CVAE only has slight improvements over CluE-baseline, does that mean the improvements are mainly from more parameters?
- In Figure 4, comparing the clustering results of the proposed model and baselines would be more convincing.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Text classification with improved embeddings
content.review:
The authors propose an improved word embedding method which takes advantage of the local context as well as the context of the entire data corpus. The proposed Clustering Enhanced neural model has two components which work in conjunction with each other: a VAE based component which refines the corpus centroids, and a biLSTM based component which uses the learnt centroids along with the local context to generate token representations. 
This is a good idea and the authors have articulated it well in the paper. They demonstrate the effectiveness of their method on several large data sets and perform a detailed empirical analysis, along with recommendations for hyperparameter selection.
A few minor concerns/suggestions for improvement: 
1. Among the comparison models, the authors should include some of the more sophisticated embedding techniques such as BERT.
2. The authors divide the results into two types: short text and long text. How are these characterized? 
3. There is an analysis of the effect of the number of clusters and number of layers the AG News dataset. The authors should at least mention how the results on the other data sets look like.
4. It would be useful to see a tabulation of the time taken for training the embeddings with the proposed method. 

Barring the above points which I hope they will address in the final version, this paper is well-written and is a significant contribution.

Discussion phase 1 edit: Having seen the other reviews, I have been convinced that there are more questions to be addressed by the authors than I saw at first reading. For instance, the feature aggregation method and the loss functions have not been justified. Though I still believe that the empirical analysis performed in the paper is very detailed, I will concede that more ablation studies are required. I have modified my rating to reflect the above.
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: review of neural text classification by joint learning of clustering and alignment
content.review:
This paper learns text classification through learning some discrete cluster vectors and how to align each tokens to the learned clusters. The paper shows that the proposed method outperforms the chosen baseline methods on some benchmarks and also delivers interpretable text representations. The authors also carry out case studies to demonstrate that the clusters help with the learning of semantic meanings. The method is clearly presented and the paper is well written. However, due to limited novelty and lack of in-depth understanding of the proposed method, I vote for rejection. 

################################################## Questions
	1. What is the input for computing clustering centers? From section 2.1, the clustering centers are learnable vectors, however, they are not quantized means of a larger observation, why is it called clusters?
	2. Does different layers share the same cluster centers? Why does the clustering-token relevances change as the embedding layer changes?
	3. What is the connection between the proposed method and vector quantized autoencoders. 
	4. Are the results in table 3 from single experiment run or multiple runs ? Please add standard deviation of the reported results. 
	5. Please add error bars in figure 3. 
What does the clusters look like with larger cluster numbers? Does the text representations are still visually separable as in Figure 4.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

display_title: The motivation is not clear and the work does not provide the sufficient experiment evidence to support the proposed method

content.title: The motivation is not clear and the work does not provide the sufficient experiment evidence to support the proposed method
content.review:
Summary:

The paper proposes a text classification model that combines BiLSTM, clustering, and Variational Autoencoder (VAE). Intuitively speaking, the method clusters each input text in the hidden space of VAE (the one having the Gaussian prior) and uses the cluster to help us to better aggregate the hidden state of BiLSTM. The experiments show that adding clustering and VAE to BiLSTM give us a slight boost on a few datasets. 



Clarity:

It is unclear why clustering and VAE are helpful in text classification. Could you give us some examples or intuitions of why we want to do that? 

Are cluster centers correspond to some topics in the input corpus? If yes, should the words closer to the topics be more important when composing the word embedding into document embedding? 
Are clustering and VAE ways to regularize the BiLSTM? There are so many other regularization methods (e.g., dropout, language modeling, weight decay, other kinds of autoencoder, etc). Why and When do you think your methods will be better than those methods? 

Combining VAE and clustering is intuitively weird. In the VAE, you encourage all the input text to have a Gaussian distribution, which suggests that you believe the embedding of each text should have only one mode. However, your method also tries to perform clustering on that space, which suggests that the embedding of each text should have multiple modes. You really need to have good motivation. Otherwise, the method would just look like a random combination of a few techniques.

The method is complicated without sufficient justification. For example, why your L_cluster is like that? Does the loss encourage each sample/text to belong to only one cluster? It is also unclear why we need to aggregate the feature using (9), (10), and (11). If your method is complicated, you need to conduct lots of ablation experiments to identify where the improvements come from. The ablation experiments might also let you discover a simpler and more effective approach.




Originality:

I indeed did not see other work that combines VAE and clustering for text classification, but there are several work that uses clustering to help text classification. In addition to the work this paper already mentioned, [1,2] are also closely related to this paper without being mentioned. Especially, [1] uses a similar idea on similar datasets and show a similar improvement.

[1] Zhang, Haidong, et al. "Cluster-Gated Convolutional Neural Network for Short Text Classification." Proceedings of the 23rd Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning (CoNLL). 2019.

[2] Gupta, Pankaj, et al. "Texttovec: Deep contextualized neural autoregressive topic models of language with distributed compositional prior." arXiv preprint arXiv:1810.03947 (2018).




Empirical contributions:

The best model in this paper only boosts a simple CNN model, TextCNN (Kim, 2014), only a little. Maybe tuning the hyperparameters of the baseline (or other baselines) on AG's News could give you a similar or better performance. The difference between CluE-baseline and CluE-CVAE is even smaller. Maybe tuning the dropout rate of CluE-baseline without using VAE could also give you a similar boost. Fig. 3a shows that the performances are similar when the number of clusters = 1 and > 1. This also increases the doubt of the effectiveness of clustering in text classification. Are all the terms in (14) necessary? What if you set lambda_3 to 0. Similarly, what about lambda_1 and lambda_2? Your method is complicated, so there are also lots of other ablation studies you can do.
You mention that your datasets come from [3], but you did not report the results on all the datasets in [3]. Why do you exclude those datasets? You have already copied the numbers from [4]. Why not also compare your methods with [4] on other datasets in [4]? There are also lots of other datasets (https://paperswithcode.com/task/text-classification). Why not try them?

The results look worse compared to the very simple methods. For example, ngrams TFIDF could achieve 7.64% error rate in AG and 1.31% in DBpedia [3]. Using pretrained LM could achieve even better results (https://paperswithcode.com/task/text-classification). Is the setting different? The datasets this paper use are also adopted by many other studies. Could you use the same setting and compare it with the numbers reported by other papers? This will reduce the chance that the poor results of baselines come from an improper setting of hyperparameters.

In Section 4.2, the authors seem to suggest that we have 4 clusters in Fig. 4 implies that adding the clustering technique is effective. However, I think the 4 clusters come from the 4 classes in this problem, which might have nothing to do with your clustering techniques. You should do the same visualization on the BiLSTM baseline and compare it with Fig. 4 to support your claims. 

Finally, I am not saying that a good paper must achieve state-of-the-art numbers, but you need to convince the reader that your method has some advantages (e.g., achieve state-of-the-art performance on smaller models; solve some limitations of state-of-the-art models in some situations). I doubt that the methods would be helpful to state-of-the-art models such as BERT because the masked word prediction task makes the model also becomes an autoencoder and pretrained language models have already provided very good regularization.

[3] Zhang, Xiang, Junbo Zhao, and Yann LeCun. "Character-level convolutional networks for text classification." Advances in neural information processing systems. 2015.

[4] Yao, Liang, Chengsheng Mao, and Yuan Luo. "Graph convolutional networks for text classification." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 33. 2019.




Significance of this work:

The paper looks like a study that heuristically combines several techniques and tricks that lead to a slightly better performance on an outdated baseline without knowing why. 



Pros:
1. Combining VAE and clustering seems to be novel (although why that is a good combination is unclear)

2. The authors seem to implement/run many baselines and show that their methods indeed achieve some performance improvement.



Cons:
1. The results are far away from state-of-the-art. The reported results are similar to simple methods such as TextCNN (Kim, 2014). The results seem to be even worse than very simple methods such as ngrams TFIDF [3].

2. Lack of ablation studies.

3. It is unclear why the proposed methods are designed like that and why they improve the BiLSTM baseline on text classification.

4. Some related work is missing



Request on the rebuttal stage:

It is unlikely that I will change my voting, so do not waste time doing rebuttal (unless you think my comments are seriously wrong. Let me know why.). I recommend directly spend time on applying the same idea to BERT and submit these results to 2nd tier conferences or journals if you really want to publish this result. If you do not have enough computational resources, try to work on distilled versions of BERT or ULMFit instead, or make your method more general and applicable to many downstream tasks.



Minor:
1. Some statements are not accurate or need more explanations/citations. For example, 
"In general, almost all NLP tasks can be cast into classification problems on either document, sentence, or word level."

2. The meaning of some descriptions is unclear. Here is an example: "Nevertheless, there remain problems that we cannot directly treat the sampled latent space of VAE for clustering centroids since there is no mechanism to modulate the representation of different samples towards different mean and variance for a better discrimination purpose under the Gaussian distribution assumption (Lim et al., 2020)".

3. In your first key contribution, why is this surprise? In your second key contribution, what do you mean "apparently capture semantic meanings"? 

4. In (8), did you use scores other than dot somewhere? If no, you don't need to mention them at all.

5. In the last paragraph of feature aggregation, you write "Fig. 2 illustrates the interaction between a^T_kt (upper-left)", but I think the upper-left matrix stores the cluster center c_k

6. What's the difference between AG's News long text and AG's News short text
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct
